SafetyAlerts
August 23, 2002
General Motors Has Recalled nearly
525,254 vehicles
(SafetyAlerts) - General Motors Corporation Has Recalled the 2000 Chevrolet Suburban, Chevrolet Tahoe, Chevrolet Tahoe, Chevrolet Silverado, GMC Yukon/Yukon XL, GMC Sierra because of airbag problems.

Number Involved: 525,254

Dates of Manufacture: February 1999 – February 2000

Defect: Some pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles have an air bag sensing diagnostic module (SDM) that contains an anomaly that could result in the driver and passenger’s air bag failing to deploy during certain frontal crashes. In a vehicle crash, front seat occupants may receive more severe injuries.

Remedy: Dealers will recalibrate the SDM in the affected vehicles. The manufacturer has reported that owner notification is expected to begin during late August 2002. Owners who do not receive the free remedy within a reasonable time should contact Chevrolet at 1-800-222-1020 or GMC at 1-800-462-8782. [NHTSA Recall No. 02V178/GM Recall No. 02029].

Important Note Regarding Auto Recalls
Frequently SafetyAlerts will list auto recalls before
your dealer will know about them. If you have a vehicle
affected by one of these posted recalls be sure and
write down the NHTSA CAMPAIGN ID Number.
If your dealer doesn't know about the recall when you
check, ask them how they are notified of recalls and
when the next update is due.

http://www.safetyalerts.com/recall/a/02/v00312.htm

I just read this and thought some of you may be interested in reading it as well:

From Pages 90-91 of the March/April '03 issue of TruckTrend

We've finally gotten an answer on the cold-start piston knock involving 4.8, 5.3 and 6.0-liter V8's in '99 to '02 GM cars and trucks. General Motors has previously released a Technical Service Bulletin explaining the condition that occurs after approximately 12,000 miles and a normal accumulation of carbon above the top piston ring.

I spoke with Sam Winegarden, GM program manager and chief engineer for small- and big-block engines. Sam explains that following extensive testing, General Motors is confident the start-up noise will have no adverse effect on performance or durability of the engines involved.

As opposed to the larger pistons of earlier design engines, today's technical refinement requires the use of smaller pistons to reduce weight and reciprocating mass in order to aid in efficiency and durability. This reduction in size also reduces the stability of the piston in the cylinder bore, which can promote piston noise.

Preliminary testing on these engines showed no sign of a problem, but, as in many other situations, the symptoms came to the surface after the vehicles were subject to normal driving conditions.

The manufacturer's stand on the issue is that it doesn't warrant a service bulletin or recall promoting a repair. We were also assured the problem has been corrected on the '03-model line with a piston-design modification along with the addition of a polymer coating.

My response was from the viewpoint of a consumer who purchased a brand-new vehicle that developed a notable engine knock before the first major service. The complaint was not only about the annoyance of the condition, but also the effect on resale and depreciation.

The answer was that General Motors would be dealing with the consumer on a case-by-case basis, and complaints have been resolved by means of warranty extension and parts replacement.

The owners of involved vehicles exhibiting the cold-start piston knock should have the service manager of the GM dealership, which has been evaluating the noise, contact the manufacturer's zone representative. Hopefully you can come to satisfactory terms.

Gentlemen,
I am new here so please dont rip my head off on my FIRST post! I am not sure I want to admit this based on this message thread, however I am a Service Manager at a UN-NAMED Chevrolet Dealership.
I have read the posts on this thread and may be able to offer some advice, confirmations and clarity!

1. I have not seen or heard of 1 single engine failure DUE to the piston problem. I did notice a post by someone about a connecting rod failure--- DIFFERENT SITUATION --! DIFFERENT SOUNDING NOISE! I can see with all the publicity of this concern how it might be confused.

2. There is also a GM TSB for a "torn" O-ring at the oil pump pickup causing aeration of the oil, the difference in the two would be that this was an assembly problem and should have been noticed from day one.

3. The good news is the noise is caused by carbon build-up on the pistons which can be "De-carbonized" and the noise will go away! The bad news is, it's like that bird that you set free, it comes back! cause it is meant to be. Again the good news is, it is just annoying!

How do you affectively de-carbonize?
During the warranty period MOST dealers will do it for you free under warranty.
If you are out of warranty the best and most effective method is:

1. Remove your spark plugs.
2. If you do not live in california, go to your local dealer and purchase "top engine clean"
3. Pour it into each cylinder.
4. LET IT SIT OVERNIGHT!
5. The next day, turn the engine over 180 degrees and pour more "Top engine clean" into each cylinder.
6. LET IT SIT OVERNIGHT!
7. Next day re-install your spark plugs.
8. Start your engine, IT WILL SMOKE AND SMELL BAD!
9. Once it stops smoking, Shut it off and CHANGE THE OIL!!
Make sure you change the oil!!! While it was sitting the Top Engine Clean was going past your rings into your crankcase!!

I like you guys own one (actually two), and I am just as unhappy with the situation as you are!

Just a little note there was for a short time, a GM TSB Listing part #'s of updated pistons for the 6.0's as they by far have the problem the worst. The part # was for the same pistons now used on the 2003.

I personally have replaced the pistons on my 6.0 and used Diamond forged pistons, and have not experienced any problems!

Sorry this is so long and I hope it helps!

rewrite.summary: This thread discusses engine knock issues in certain Chevrolet and GMC models, as well as recalls for fuel system and body door hinge assemblies. General Motors has addressed the engine knock by providing a technical service bulletin (TSB) recommending carbon cleaning.
seo_outline: General Motors' Response to Engine Knocks
rewrite.rewritten_article_markdown:
In 2002, General Motors recalled nearly 525,254 vehicles including the 2000 Chevrolet Suburban, Tahoe, Silverado, GMC Yukon/Yukon XL, and Sierra due to airbag problems. Additionally, in 2003, several models were recalled for fuel system and body door hinge issues.

Engine knock at start-up has been reported by owners of certain GM vehicles from 1999 to 2002. General Motors addressed this concern with a technical service bulletin (TSB) explaining that the noise is due to carbon build-up on pistons. The manufacturer states that it does not warrant a recall or repair, but dealers will offer free de-carbonization services under warranty.

For the fuel and door hinge issues in 2003 models, the recalls involve Chevrolet Suburban, Tahoe, Yukon/Yukon XL, and GMC Sierra and Yukon. Dealers will inspect and correct any issues identified during vehicle checks.

General Motors has recalled nearly 525,254 vehicles, including 2000 Chevrolet Suburban, Tahoe, Silverado, GMC Yukon/Yukon XL, and Sierra models due to potential airbag issues. The recall covers vehicles manufactured from February 1999 to February 2000.

The defect involves an anomaly in the air bag sensing diagnostic module (SDM) that may prevent the driver and passenger airbags from deploying during certain frontal crashes. This could result in more severe injuries for front seat occupants.

GM dealers will recalibrate the SDM in affected vehicles. Notification to owners is expected to begin in late August 2002. Contact Chevrolet at 1-800-222-1020 or GMC at 1-800-462-8782 if you do not receive the remedy within a reasonable time.

Important: SafetyAlerts often publish recalls before dealers are notified, so check for your vehicle's NHTSA CAMPAIGN ID Number. Ask your dealer about their recall notification process and update schedule.

GMC has recalled the 2003 Yukon, Yukon XL, Suburban, and Avalanche due to potential issues with the fuel system, specifically the gasoline storage tank assembly. Additionally, a separate recall involves these same models for structural concerns related to door hinges and attachments. For more details, see the following safety alerts:
- Fuel System Recall: <http://www.safetyalerts.com/recall/a/02/v00586.htm>
- Structure Recall: <http://www.safetyalerts.com/recall/a/02/v00570.htm>

From pages 90-91 of the March/April '03 issue of TruckTrend, an answer was finally provided regarding cold-start piston knock in 4.8, 5.3, and 6.0-liter V8 engines from '99 to '02 GM vehicles. Sam Winegarden, GM's program manager for small- and big-block engines, explained that extensive testing has shown the noise will not affect engine performance or durability. Smaller pistons, designed for reduced weight and improved efficiency, are more prone to noise due to less stability in the cylinder bore. While initial tests showed no issues, symptoms emerged under normal driving conditions. GM does not consider this a reason for a service bulletin or recall.

A piston design modification and polymer coating were introduced in the '03 model year to address the issue. For consumers who experienced significant engine knock before major service, General Motors will handle complaints on a case-by-case basis, often through warranty extensions and part replacements. Owners of affected vehicles should contact their GM dealership's zone representative for further assistance.
Great news! Moving forward with Option 03.

I've been informed by reliable sources that the issue lies with the cheap piston manufacturer. This appears to be a significant problem, though it may not be critical. It seems like a major oversight on someone's part, and it's concerning for both face and financial reasons.

I recently purchased a 2001 Sierra with a 5.3L engine, which developed a knocking sound. The dealer initially attributed this to cheap gas or carbon buildup, but after overnight idling and a cold start, the connecting rod broke, causing significant damage to the block. They replaced it with a complete motor assembly.

The new motor, now eight months old, is also producing a knock. After returning it, dealership technicians claimed no noticeable noise. However, I detected knocking and was dismissed. I am currently contacting customer service for further assistance.

It’s important not to attribute knocks solely to carbon buildup. The design of these motors with loose piston skirts and higher tolerances for power output can lead to excessive play in connecting rods and uneven wear on cylinder walls and pistons, similar to racing setups where components are built looser for more power but require more frequent rebuilds.
I believe GM is attempting to delay accountability by pushing this issue until the engines are out of warranty. I plan to share this with my machinist.

I suggest picking up a combustion chamber cleaner to address any piston issues. It costs around $20 or less and can resolve problems caused by carbon buildup. If the issue persists, it might indicate motor problems. This is a simple tool I frequently use to fix knocking noises due to carbon deposits, especially common in Jeep V8 engines.

My 1999 Yukon Denali experiences a cold-start knocking issue, which persists even at 99,000 miles. I initially feared the engine was failing but am relieved to learn it fades away within about 30 seconds of driving.
CSK... visit TSB's guide at [http://www.pistonslap.com/tsb.htm](http://www.pistonslap.com/tsb.htm)

TireFryer, I've noticed many cycling switches malfunctioning. This switch is located on the accumulator (the long cylinder near the passenger side firewall). If the A/C blows warm air, check if the compressor clutch is engaged. Try tapping on the switch or wiggling its connector to see if it engages the clutch.

There is a bulletin (#02-01-38-007) that details additional AC performance checks for technicians dealing with poor A/C issues. For 2003 XL models, there are no specific recalls related to A/C problems. However, there is a bulletin (bulletin #01-01-39-004A) addressing poor A/C performance at idle or in traffic, which recommends installing an auxiliary electric fan.

I am a new Service Manager at an unnamed Chevrolet dealership and I may be able to provide some insight based on the posts here. 

1. There has been no engine failure due to the piston issue reported; however, there was a post about a connecting rod failure—different situation and noise.

2. A GM TSB addresses an "torn" O-ring at the oil pump pickup causing oil aeration. This is an assembly problem that should have been noticed initially.

3. The noise you’re experiencing is due to carbon buildup on the pistons, which can be removed ("decarbonized"), but it returns over time.

Decarbonizing effectively:
1. Remove spark plugs.
2. Purchase "top engine clean" from your local dealer (non-California).
3. Pour into each cylinder and let sit overnight.
4. Turn engine 180 degrees and pour more "top engine clean."
5. Let it sit overnight again.
6. Re-install spark plugs, start the engine; expect smoke and foul smell.
7. Once stopped smoking, change oil.

A GM TSB listed part numbers for updated pistons, which I replaced with Diamond forged ones on my 2003 model without issues.

Thank you for your understanding!

Piston-slap occurs in new 5.3 V-8 engines, particularly during cool morning starts (in the low 70s). While I don't experience this issue personally, it can be heard as a snapping sound when starting these vehicles. Although it doesn't necessarily indicate a problem, it can be an annoyance for owners and may deter potential buyers due to its unusual start-up noise. Even if it doesn’t cause damage, the sound can be distressing and reflects poorly on GM’s attention to engine aural quality at startup.

Does Tech Service Bulletin (TSB) #01-01-39-004A apply to my 2003 Silverado? At highway speeds, the air conditioning blows cold with vent temperatures around 45-50°F. When parked, the vent temperatures are about 70-75°F. Since a faulty low pressure switch has been replaced, could this symptom indicate another issue? Any insights would be appreciated.
